sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

inspect:2611.17191.question: In the mixed-domain LoRA rank sweeps, what are the unpenalized LoRA baselines, model sizes, evaluation metrics, and per-rank results for the Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer? passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

Standard LoRA training often underutilizes its allocated subspace so nominal rank is an unreliable proxy for usable adapter capacity in the learning–forgetting trade-off. Our single-task and scheduling experiments also demonstrate configuration-dependent learning and retention outcomes: the penalty can improve retention without a large training-fit cost, but does not eliminate the learning–forgetting trade-off. Spectral diagnostics provide descriptive comparisons of the resulting updates. Effective rank is therefore not merely a post-hoc diagnostic but a trainable objective that regularizes toward fuller utilization.

Wiki PPL and StarCoder PPL are reference-probe perplexities on fixed OLMo-Mix-1124 slices, using the plain-text supervision protocol and batch limits specified above. In the mixed-domain setting we additionally log in-mixture retention probes on held-out GSM8K and WMT19 Czech–English validation text; Appendix Table 5 reports both in-mixture probes. eRank is the Roy–Vetterli effective rank of the accumulated adapter update Δ ​ W \Delta W , averaged over all targeted down_proj modules, taken from the last logged rank diagnostic. This is distinct from the Rényi-2 surrogate used in the objective. Dense down-projection fine-tuning baselines select hyperparameters via a separate sweep (Section F.1 ), but reported metrics still refer to the terminal state of the selected run. Post-hoc spectral analyses (intruder dimensions, subspace alignment, singular-direction mixing) use measurements from the final saved checkpoint.

passages.text: These sweeps examine how the learning–retention balance changes with the configured rank and penalty weight. Fuller spectral utilization need not improve every perplexity metric, so effective rank should be interpreted jointly with mixture fit and the held-out probes.

inspect:2611.16905.question: In LLM pretraining experiments, what model sizes, token budgets, hardware, and baselines are used to compare FOAM with SOAP, Muon, and AdamW? What are the measured optimizer-state memory, peak GPU memory, wall-clock throughput, and validation-loss results, and are comparisons made at matched training compute?

passages.text: Second-order optimizers ( e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP’s dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP’s dense second moment, and we measure only a 15–20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP’s optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP’s gains need not require SOAP’s cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam . $\star$ $\star$ footnotetext: Correspondence to {jaemyung.yu, dongyoon.han}@navercorp.com

Concretely, our approach is built on two structural simplifications: input-only preconditioning and a factored Adam-Moment update. The first simplification drops the output-side factor L L and retains only the input-side factor R R , eliminating its m 2 m^{2} memory and one of the two eigendecompositions. Its justification follows from the Kronecker structure of the Hessian, in which all output rows of an affine layer share the same input-side outer product x ​ x ⊤ xx^{\top} [ 25 ] , while the Hessian of transformer layers is empirically near-block-diagonal along output neurons or heads [ 50 ] , making the input-only form the natural one-sided approximation. The second simplification replaces the dense rotated second moment with a row-and-column factored estimator, r ∈ ℝ m r\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and c ∈ ℝ n c\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , with trace normalization, reducing the buffer size from m ​ n mn to m + n m+n . Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption [ 35 ] with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP’s dense second moment, and the K-FAC part holds to a 15 15 – 20 % 20\% relative error in practice. Together, these simplifications reduce SOAP’s optimizer state from 2 ​ m ​ n + 2 ​ m 2 + 2 ​ n 2 2mn+2m^{2}+2n^{2} to m ​ n + 2 ​ n 2 + m + n mn+2n^{2}+m+n and the amortized eigendecomposition count from two to one. We call the resulting method FOAM ( F actored O ne-sided A dam- M oment).

Figure 1 highlights FOAM’s main advantages. On pre-training, FOAM matches the strong Muon and SOAP baselines on validation loss with half of SOAP’s optimizer state and reaches AdamW’s final loss within 7 % 7\% of AdamW’s own wall-clock time , while SOAP needs more than twice as long at 760M, and FOAM matches AdamW’s hyperparameter robustness over a three-fold learning-rate range. The advantage holds from 124M to 760M parameters with learning rates re-tuned at every size from a μ \mu P [ 46 ] anchor. In summary, our contributions are: (i) a structural justification of input-only preconditioning, with the Kronecker structure of the Hessian and empirical verifications with LLMs with recent architectural elements; (ii) a factored Adam-Moment update with trace normalization, exact under K-FAC with a diagonal output curvature and empirically validated through K-FAC-residual measurements during training; and (iii) the resulting algorithm FOAM, a scalable and practical SOAP variant that delivers SOAP-class quality with half of SOAP’s optimizer state ( + 7.4 % +7.4\% measured peak training memory over AdamW) and Muon-class wall-clock time.

Table 2 reports the main pre-training results across three model scales. SOAP attains the lowest validation loss at every scale, with FOAM behind by 0.004 0.004 , 0.008 0.008 , and 0.005 0.005 nats at small, medium, and large, each within about one seed std. FOAM is ahead of Muon, AdaMuon, and AdamW at every scale. The cost gap to SOAP widens at scale . FOAM uses half of SOAP’s matrix-parameter state at every size, and its measured peak memory at small size is + 7.4 % +7.4\% over AdamW against + 12.9 % +12.9\% for SOAP. On wall-clock time, FOAM needs fewer steps than AdamW to reach AdamW’s final loss, which offsets its higher per-step cost: its time to that loss, t A t_{\mathrm{A}} , is within 7 % 7\% of AdamW’s own at every scale and equal at large ( 10.53 10.53 vs. 10.55 10.55 h), whereas SOAP needs 1.35 × 1.35\times at small and 2.15 × 2.15\times at large, as its two eigendecompositions grow cubically with width.

Limitations and future work. Our experiments stop at GPT-2 scale, up to 1.56B parameters, so whether FOAM’s advantages hold for frontier-scale pre-training remains the main open question. Our implementation does not yet shard R R and Q R Q_{R} across devices, which matters at the ≥ 7 \geq 7 B scale, although the layer-wise distributed optimizer of Khona et al. [22] suggests that this is an engineering rather than a fundamental obstacle. The factored update is least accurate at the key projection, whose gradients pass through RoPE and softmax (Appendix C ). Finally, the embeddings and the lm-head stay on AdamW because their vocabulary dimension rules out a dense factor on that side, although a FOAM-style factor on their small hidden dimension would be affordable. Extending FOAM to these layers, and attention-aware factorizations for the key projection, are natural next steps. When to use FOAM. FOAM fits when SOAP-class quality is needed but SOAP’s memory or wall-clock is binding, since it stays within 0.004 0.004 – 0.008 0.008 nats of SOAP at half its optimizer state and, at 760M, about half its wall-clock. Against Muon and AdaMuon, quality slightly favors FOAM at every scale and speed is near parity, while AdaMuon keeps less state. Muon and AdaMuon thus remain preferable when optimizer state is the hardest constraint. Against AdamW, FOAM, like other matrix-preconditioned methods, is most valuable at large effective batch, where AdamW degrades (Appendix G ) and, at fixed 𝚙𝚏 \mathtt{pf} , the optimizer’s compute share shrinks. FOAM is least attractive when memory is dominated by modules with a large input dimension, such as the MLP down-projection, whose n 2 n^{2} factor carries most of FOAM’s residual state over AdamW.

Conclusion. We presented FOAM , a scalable and practical SOAP variant built on two structural simplifications: input-only preconditioning, justified by the Kronecker structure of the Hessian and a near-diagonal output curvature, and a factored Adam-Moment update, exact under K-FAC, with Purifying Shampoo’s skip rule for the amortized eigenbasis update. Where memory-efficient variants mainly shrink AdamW’s memory, FOAM addresses the complementary problem and brings SOAP-level quality close to Adam-level cost. FOAM matches strong Muon and SOAP baselines on LLM pre-training with modern architectures while using half of SOAP’s optimizer state and Muon-level wall-clock time, from 124M to 760M , with supporting evidence at 1.56B and on ViT.

Our implementation does not yet shard R R and Q R Q_{R} across devices, which matters at the ≥ 7 \geq 7 B scale, although the layer-wise distributed optimizer of Khona et al. [22] suggests that this is an engineering rather than a fundamental obstacle. The factored update is least accurate at the key projection, whose gradients pass through RoPE and softmax (Appendix C ). Extending FOAM to these layers, and attention-aware factorizations for the key projection, are natural next steps. When to use FOAM. FOAM fits when SOAP-class quality is needed but SOAP’s memory or wall-clock is binding, since it stays within 0.004 0.004 – 0.008 0.008 nats of SOAP at half its optimizer state and, at 760M, about half its wall-clock. FOAM is least attractive when memory is dominated by modules with a large input dimension, such as the MLP down-projection, whose n 2 n^{2} factor carries most of FOAM’s residual state over AdamW.

Conclusion. We presented FOAM , a scalable and practical SOAP variant built on two structural simplifications: input-only preconditioning, justified by the Kronecker structure of the Hessian and a near-diagonal output curvature, and a factored Adam-Moment update, exact under K-FAC, with Purifying Shampoo’s skip rule for the amortized eigenbasis update. Where memory-efficient variants mainly shrink AdamW’s memory, FOAM addresses the complementary problem and brings SOAP-level quality close to Adam-level cost. FOAM matches strong Muon and SOAP baselines on LLM pre-training with modern architectures while using half of SOAP’s optimizer state and Muon-level wall-clock time, from 124M to 760M , with supporting evidence at 1.56B and on ViT.

passages.text: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR , which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. The combination of adaptation quality, a compact trainable state, and training efficiency makes SCALAR a promising approach to resource-constrained fine-tuning. 1 1 footnotetext: Work done during an internship at OPPO AI-Center. 1 1 footnotetext: National University of Defense Technology. Contact: suntao.saltfish@outlook.com 2 2 footnotetext: OPPO AI center

How can we construct a task-relevant fixed update space that maintains adaptation quality with few trainable coefficients, low memory use, and high throughput? We first investigate this question through a learned-direction reweighting diagnostic. We train a rank-one LoRA adapter, freeze its learned update direction for each adapted matrix, and re-optimize one scalar coefficient per matrix. On a 7B model, the reweighting stage optimizes 196 196 parameters compared with LoRA’s 2,523,136 2{,}523{,}136 , and achieves similar optimization behavior and downstream accuracy. This observation motivates constructing informative directions before fine-tuning and adapting through a small set of coefficients. We propose SCALAR : Subspace-Calibrated Adaptation via Layerwise Atom Reweighting . SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from the leading singular vectors of downstream activations and assigns a separate random output dictionary to each input direction. Learning the coefficients selects an effective output vector within each of these fixed output subspaces. With R R input directions and H H output atoms per direction, each adapted matrix has K = R ​ H K=RH trainable coefficients and an update rank of at most R R . The output atoms in each group are aggregated before application to the activations, so the token-dependent matrix multiplications operate on R R effective directions. Compatible layers can also share the frozen output dictionaries.

Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, and code generation show competitive performance with compact trainable budgets. On Qwen2.5-7B and LLaMA3-8B, SCALAR approaches rank-8 LoRA accuracy on commonsense reasoning using about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements demonstrate lower peak training memory and higher throughput, giving the compact parameterization practical value during training. Our analysis builds on activation coverage to examine the initial gradient signal and connects it to the coefficients trained by SCALAR . (a) Qwen2.5-7B (b) LLaMA3-8B Figure 1 : Average accuracy on 8 commonsense reasoning tasks across trainable parameter budgets. SCALAR approaches LoRA-level accuracy with substantially fewer trainable parameters. Our main contributions are summarized as follows. Task-calibrated fixed-subspace adaptation. We introduce SCALAR , which combines an activation-derived input basis with a separate random output subspace for each input direction. Its grouped parameterization learns R ​ H RH coefficients and applies the update through R R aggregated output vectors. Compatible layers share their fixed output dictionaries to reduce basis storage. Analysis and diagnostic evidence. Building on activation-subspace analysis, we characterize the effect of gradient-weighted activation geometry on the initial learning signal and derive its connection to SCALAR ’s coefficients. A learned-direction reweighting diagnostic motivates adaptation within informative fixed update spaces.

We evaluate adaptation quality at compact trainable budgets and measure the corresponding training memory and throughput. The experiments cover several language adaptation tasks. The Appendix includes additional diagnostic analyses, comparisons with enhanced LoRA variants, general instruction fine-tuning, larger-model evaluations, and extensive ablations on the parameterization, calibration, rank, initialization, and cross-layer sharing, together with full implementation details and parameter-budget comparisons. Training Configuration. We evaluate SCALAR on commonsense reasoning with Qwen2.5 Yang et al. (2024a) and LLaMA3 Grattafiori et al. (2024) , and further test transfer to mathematical reasoning and code generation. We also ablate the initialization of the fixed bases 𝑨 \bm{A} and 𝑩 \bm{B} . Baselines. We compare SCALAR with full-parameter fine-tuning and five representative PEFT methods: Full Fine-tuning (FT) as a full-capacity reference; LoRA Hu et al. (2022) , the standard trainable low-rank parameterization; VeRA Kopiczko et al. (2024) , which shares random low-rank projections and learns layer-specific scaling vectors; LoRA-XS Bałazy et al. (2024) , which optimizes a compact matrix between fixed projections; NOLA Koohpayegani et al. (2024) , which learns combinations of fixed random bases; and RandLoRA Albert et al. (2025) , which aggregates random low-rank bases with trainable diagonal scalings.

(a) Memory comparison (b) Training tokens/s Figure 2 : Memory and throughput for fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B on commonsense reasoning. We report peak GPU memory with a device batch size of 16 and token throughput on 2 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. SCALAR uses less memory and achieves higher throughput than the compared baselines. Figure 2 compares peak GPU memory and training token throughput when fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B. SCALAR achieves the lowest peak memory among the evaluated PEFT methods, using 20% less memory than LoRA, 15% less than NOLA, and 33% less than RandLoRA. Training throughput increases by 6% over LoRA, 34% over NOLA, and approximately 130% over RandLoRA. Together with the accuracy results, these measurements show that SCALAR combines a compact trainable budget with effective adaptation, lower peak memory, and higher throughput. The structural ablations in Appendix C.6.1 examine how grouped computation and cross-layer dictionary sharing balance accuracy and training cost.

passages.text: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ) with Federated Learning ( FL ) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ( 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and 𝐁 \mathbf{B} ) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen 𝐀 \mathbf{A} matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling 𝐀 \mathbf{A} matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and 𝐁 \mathbf{B} gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. In this work, we studied language-model post-training by separating the structure of cumulative weight updates from the directions of successive training displacements. Our power-law construction showed that low stable rank and large fixed-energy rank are mathematically compatible, and full decompositions verified this separation in selected OLMo-2-7B updates. A dominant singular value can therefore coexist with hundreds of components needed to retain most of an update’s energy. This distinction clarifies why different rank measures can give contrasting descriptions of the same matrix. Trajectory measurements add information about how successive weight changes interact. All 131 measured adjacent pairs across nine public RLVR stages from the OLMo-2, OLMoE, and Olmo-3 releases had negative cosine on their native checkpoint grids, including PPO and GRPO releases. Supervised comparisons of OLMo-2-7B, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3 showed configuration-dependent alignment, with late anti-alignment in Mistral and FP32 Llama runs. In a three-seed matched RL study initialized from OLMo-2-0425-1B-DPO and trained on the RLVR-GSM mathematical-answer dataset, replacing group-relative advantages with the critic–GAE package consistently lowered alignment under a shared actor schedule. Together, these findings support a more precise account of post-training geometry. Spectral concentration, energy coverage, and trajectory direction answer different questions and should be reported separately. passages.text: Transmitting LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training over bandwidth-constrained networks. Lowering the training rank may limit the capacity a workload needs, while adaptive optimizer updates are difficult to compress. Rollout workers can instead reconstruct updates from gradients by maintaining replicated optimizer states. We introduce HiLo , a compressor-agnostic framework that replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay. By applying the same decoded gradients, the learner and workers maintain consistent policy states at the same version under reproducible execution. We further develop Spar , a budget-aware gradient compressor that combines spectral truncation, adaptive rank allocation and error feedback to decouple training rank from communication cost. Experiments across on-policy distillation and reward-guided post-training show that HiLo with Spar maintains learning quality close to full synchronization while transmitting as little as 1.6% of the adapter bytes, and accelerates end-to-end updates by up to 2.2 × 2.2\times under bandwidth constraints.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning, particularly Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , reduces the synchronization payload to the adapter factors, whose size scales with the training rank. Synchronization can remain expensive over bandwidth-constrained WANs, especially when many workers share the learner’s uplink ( Song et al., 2026 ) . Although lowering the training rank reduces this cost, it also restricts the space of learnable weight updates. The rank needed for effective adaptation varies across workloads and adapted modules ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , with very low ranks sufficient in some RL settings but inadequate for supervised fine-tuning or continued pretraining in others ( Biderman et al., 2024 ; Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ) . Ideally, the rank should be determined by the learning workload, while synchronization cost should be controlled independently by the network budget. Recent work reduces synchronization traffic by losslessly encoding differences between consecutive policy snapshots. SparseRL-Sync transmits changed values and their indices ( Hu et al., 2026 ) , while ARC exploits unchanged values and bit-level redundancy ( Fireworks AI, 2026 ) . These methods preserve the BF16 snapshots exactly and can achieve substantial savings when rounding leaves many weights unchanged. Their payloads, however, depend on the changes that must be preserved and the redundancy available to the codec. Consequently, lossless encoding alone does not guarantee a prescribed per-update communication budget.

We therefore ask whether synchronization must operate on parameter changes at all. For a gradient-driven optimizer with reproducible transitions, the next state is determined by the current parameters, optimizer state, gradient and update configuration. Distributed data-parallel training uses this principle to keep replicas synchronized through shared gradients and local optimizer updates ( Li et al., 2020 ) . A rollout worker can likewise reconstruct the learner’s update from the same gradient by maintaining replicated parameters and optimizer state under matched execution. This moves compression before the optimizer step, allowing established gradient-compression methods ( Lin et al., 2018 ; Vogels et al., 2019 ) to exploit gradient structure before optimizer transformations reshape the update (§ 3.3 ). Building on this insight, we introduce HiLo ( Hi gh-rank in training, Lo w-rank on the wire), a framework for communication-efficient LoRA synchronization in distributed on-policy post-training. HiLo replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay, reducing synchronization traffic without lowering the training rank. We further develop Spar (Spectral Packing with Adaptive Ranks), a budget-aware gradient compressor tailored to LoRA that serves as a backend for HiLo. Together, HiLo and Spar alleviate the synchronization bottleneck, allowing distributed rollout to scale more effectively over bandwidth-constrained networks. Our main contributions are as follows.

• We formalize HiLo as a compressor-agnostic optimizer-replay protocol and establish conditions for matching learner and worker parameters and optimizer states at the same policy version. This enables different gradient-compression backends to plug into the same synchronization protocol while preserving same-version consistency. • We design Spar to compress LoRA-factor gradients using spectral truncation via small Gram-matrix eigendecompositions, global rank allocation under a byte budget, and error feedback. The resulting allocation prioritizes gradient directions with the highest spectral value per communicated byte. • We evaluate HiLo on two reasoning tasks and test robustness across four optimizers. With Spar, HiLo maintains accuracy close to full synchronization at 1.6% of the adapter bytes and achieves up to 2.2 × 2.2\times end-to-end speedup on bandwidth-limited links. inspect:2611.14397.question: Does MaLoRA evaluate its margin and adapter-merging predictions in language-model fine-tuning, beyond multiclass linear classification? What models, tasks, baselines, and measured forgetting or merging results are reported?

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks, achieving strong task adaptation with minimal trainable parameters and low optimization cost. Beyond this efficiency, practitioners have observed two striking properties: robustness to catastrophic forgetting and the ability to merge independently trained adapters into a single model that performs competitively across multiple tasks. These properties are central to continual and multi-task learning, yet remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a theoretical explanation through a unified margin-based perspective . We analyze LoRA in multiclass linear classification under a near-orthogonal task regime with ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -regularization, and characterize the optimal LoRA adapter across regularization regimes. Our analysis shows that, in an intermediate regime of regularization parameters, the optimal adapter aligns with the max-margin solution on the fine-tuning data. Building on this characterization, we derive two key consequences. First, we obtain closed-form expressions for the margins on pre-training and fine-tuning data, revealing a precise margin trade-off: the regularization parameter controls the balance between retention and adaptation. Second, we analyze adapter merging, proving that merged models achieve positive margin on each task and deriving optimal mixing coefficients that balance margins across tasks and maximize the margin over their union. These results lead to a simple, training-free merging rule, which we term margin-based LoRA merging (MaLoRA). Experiments on modern architectures and real datasets validate our theoretical predictions, showing that MaLoRA matches or outperforms several adapter-merging baselines across a range of

ing (MaLoRA). Experiments on modern architectures and real datasets validate our theoretical predictions, showing that MaLoRA matches or outperforms several adapter-merging baselines across a range of vision and language classification tasks.

• Theory for reduced forgetting. We define forgetting as the reduction in margin on the pre-training data after fine-tuning, and derive closed-form expressions for the normalized margins on the pre-training data, the fine-tuning data, and their union (Theorem 3.2 ). Our analysis shows that these margins are governed by the regularization parameter and satisfy a precise trade-off: decreasing the regularization parameter increases the fine-tuning margin but also increases the Frobenius-norm ratio of the adapter to the pre-trained weights, leading to greater forgetting. We further identify the regularization parameter that maximizes the margin on the union of pre-training and fine-tuning tasks, thereby optimally balancing retention and adaptation. • Theory for adapter merging. Under the intermediate-regime assumption for each task, we derive closed-form expressions for the margin of the merged model on every task (Theorem 3.3 ). We show that the merged model attains strictly positive margin on each task, providing a theoretical explanation for the effectiveness of adapter merging. We also characterize, in closed form, the mixing coefficients that maximize the margin of the merged model on the union of all tasks, which naturally leads to margin-based LoRA merging (MaLoRA), a theoretically motivated adapter-merging method. This contrasts with many existing model-merging approaches, which rely primarily on heuristic prescriptions for choosing how to combine task-specific models.

Our experiments aim to validate the theoretical predictions in Section 3 and assess how well they transfer beyond the linear setting, rather than to establish state-of-the-art performance. Since our analysis gives closed-form predictions for optimal regularization and adapter mixing coefficients, we test whether these quantities match empirical behavior in modern architectures. Specifically, we focus on two questions: (i) whether the mixing coefficients derived from our margin analysis agree with empirically optimal coefficients, and (ii) whether the resulting theory-driven merging rule, MaLoRA, remains competitive with adapter-merging baselines in nonlinear models. Experiments on the effect of regularization are deferred to Appendix H.1.2 .

Setup and metric. We evaluate our theory and method in two complementary settings. First, in linear probing on CIFAR-100 ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) (§ 4.1 ), we use four frozen pre-trained backbones ( ResNet-50 , ViT-B/16 , ConvNeXt , and CLIP ) as feature extractors ( He et al., 2016 ; Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ; Radford et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) , apply LoRA only to the final linear classifier ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) , and construct tasks from the CIFAR-100 superclass hierarchy. Second, in multi-domain adapter merging (§ 4.2 ), we evaluate ViT-B/16 on PACS, VLCS, and TerraIncognita ( Fang et al., 2013 ; Li et al., 2017 ; Beery et al., 2018 ) , and XLM-RoBERTa Base on MNLI, Amazon Reviews, and CivilComments ( Zhang et al., 2015 ; Williams et al., 2018 ; Borkan et al., 2019 ; Conneau et al., 2020 ) . Although our theory is stated in terms of normalized margin, we report classification accuracy in experiments, since real-world classification tasks often do not achieve perfect separation and can have negative normalized margins. Additional details are given in Appendix H .

In this work, we study LoRA fine-tuning through the normalized margin under a near-orthogonal task regime. We characterize the global minimizer of the regularized LoRA objective across three regularization regimes (Theorem 3.1 ), derive closed-form expressions for the margins on the pre-training and fine-tuning data, and identify the regularization level that maximizes the margin on their union (Theorem 3.2 ). We further extend the analysis to multi-task settings by deriving closed-form optimal mixing coefficients for adapter merging (Theorem 3.3 ). Based on this theory, we propose margin-based LoRA merging (MaLoRA, Algorithm 1 ), which matches or outperforms several adapter-merging baselines on a range of vision and language benchmarks. Across architectures and tasks, the empirical results closely align with the theoretical predictions. Limitations and future work. First, our analysis relies on simplifying assumptions, most notably near-orthogonal task structure (Assumption 2.1 ) and balanced class sizes in the fine-tuning data. These assumptions enable a sharp closed-form characterization, but they also limit the scope of the theory. An important direction for future work is to relax them and study LoRA under more general data distributions and pre-training conditions. Second, experiments applying MaLoRA to nonlinear models provide empirical support for the practical usefulness of our merging rule beyond multiclass linear classification. These findings motivate extending the margin-based theoretical analysis to nonlinear adaptation. Third, our theory characterizes margins on the training datasets; establishing corresponding generalization or test-risk guarantees requires further analysis.

We further identify the regularization parameter that maximizes the margin on the union of pre-training and fine-tuning tasks, thereby optimally balancing retention and adaptation. • Theory for adapter merging. Under the intermediate-regime assumption for each task, we derive closed-form expressions for the margin of the merged model on every task (Theorem 3.3 ). We show that the merged model attains strictly positive margin on each task, providing a theoretical explanation for the effectiveness of adapter merging. We also characterize, in closed form, the mixing coefficients that maximize the margin of the merged model on the union of all tasks, which naturally leads to margin-based LoRA merging (MaLoRA), a theoretically motivated adapter-merging method. This contrasts with many existing model-merging approaches, which rely primarily on heuristic prescriptions for choosing how to combine task-specific models.

Our experiments aim to validate the theoretical predictions in Section 3 and assess how well they transfer beyond the linear setting, rather than to establish state-of-the-art performance. Since our analysis gives closed-form predictions for optimal regularization and adapter mixing coefficients, we test whether these quantities match empirical behavior in modern architectures. Specifically, we focus on two questions: (i) whether the mixing coefficients derived from our margin analysis agree with empirically optimal coefficients, and (ii) whether the resulting theory-driven merging rule, MaLoRA, remains competitive with adapter-merging baselines in nonlinear models. Experiments on the effect of regularization are deferred to Appendix H.1.2 .

Setup and metric. We evaluate our theory and method in two complementary settings. First, in linear probing on CIFAR-100 ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) (§ 4.1 ), we use four frozen pre-trained backbones ( ResNet-50 , ViT-B/16 , ConvNeXt , and CLIP ) as feature extractors ( He et al., 2016 ; Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ; Radford et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) , apply LoRA only to the final linear classifier ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) , and construct tasks from the CIFAR-100 superclass hierarchy. Second, in multi-domain adapter merging (§ 4.2 ), we evaluate ViT-B/16 on PACS, VLCS, and TerraIncognita ( Fang et al., 2013 ; Li et al., 2017 ; Beery et al., 2018 ) , and XLM-RoBERTa Base on MNLI, Amazon Reviews, and CivilComments ( Zhang et al., 2015 ; Williams et al., 2018 ; Borkan et al., 2019 ; Conneau et al., 2020 ) . Although our theory is stated in terms of normalized margin, we report classification accuracy in experiments, since real-world classification tasks often do not achieve perfect separation and can have negative normalized margins. Additional details are given in Appendix H .

In this work, we study LoRA fine-tuning through the normalized margin under a near-orthogonal task regime. We characterize the global minimizer of the regularized LoRA objective across three regularization regimes (Theorem 3.1 ), derive closed-form expressions for the margins on the pre-training and fine-tuning data, and identify the regularization level that maximizes the margin on their union (Theorem 3.2 ). We further extend the analysis to multi-task settings by deriving closed-form optimal mixing coefficients for adapter merging (Theorem 3.3 ). Based on this theory, we propose margin-based LoRA merging (MaLoRA, Algorithm 1 ), which matches or outperforms several adapter-merging baselines on a range of vision and language benchmarks. Across architectures and tasks, the empirical results closely align with the theoretical predictions. Limitations and future work. First, our analysis relies on simplifying assumptions, most notably near-orthogonal task structure (Assumption 2.1 ) and balanced class sizes in the fine-tuning data. These assumptions enable a sharp closed-form characterization, but they also limit the scope of the theory. An important direction for future work is to relax them and study LoRA under more general data distributions and pre-training conditions. Second, experiments applying MaLoRA to nonlinear models provide empirical support for the practical usefulness of our merging rule beyond multiclass linear classification. These findings motivate extending the margin-based theoretical analysis to nonlinear adaptation. Third, our theory characterizes margins on the training datasets; establishing corresponding generalization or test-risk guarantees requires further analysis.

passages.text: The implicit-bias literature studies how optimization selects a solution among the many parameter settings that fit the training data. Such selection has been characterized for steepest descent under different norms ( Gunasekar et al., 2018 ) and for product parameterizations with small initialization ( Woodworth et al., 2020 ) . On grokking tasks, parameterization scale affects feature learning ( Kumar et al., 2024 ) , and the optimizer affects whether grokking occurs ( Thilak et al., 2022 ) . With adaptive optimizers, an L2 penalty added to the gradient is rescaled together with it, so parameters with small gradients are regularized more strongly than under decoupled weight decay ( Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019 ) . We connect this selection to circuit concentration through a controlled intervention on credit allocation.

If per-neuron normalization is what distributes the circuit, optimizers should sort accordingly. We train with the eight optimizers of Table 1 that replace Adam. LARS, RMSProp, LAMB, Adafactor, Lion, Muon and Shampoo normalize groups other than a single neuron or change update directions, and all seven produce concentrated circuits, with participation between 0.470 0.470 and 0.613 0.613 . All seven run with the coupled weight decay of the reference. Nero, which uses no weight decay, produces at its default learning rate of 10 − 2 10^{-2} a distributed circuit with participation 0.986 0.986 at test accuracy 0.985 0.985 (Table 13 ). Nero, which normalizes credit per neuron, and DFC, whose credit is nearly equal (credit participation 0.94 0.94 ), are cases of equal credit that arise without our intervention, and both produce distributed circuits. For the reference, DFC and the equalization sweeps, credit participation lies close to circuit participation (Figure 3 a). The condition also explains why equal update norms do not suffice. Lion gives every neuron an update of the same norm, and Adam-mini ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) normalizes each neuron’s update with one second-moment estimate, yet both keep the circuit concentrated (Adam-mini 0.586 0.586 against 0.594 0.594 for Adam, Appendix D.1 ). Both normalize the coupled decay together with the gradient, so each neuron’s ratio of credit to decay is unchanged.

Figure 3: Circuit participation under different transformations of the learning signal. (a) Circuit participation against credit participation for the reference, DFC, credit equalization at β = 0.25 \beta=0.25 and β = 1 \beta=1 , the group-size sweep on four tasks and seven optimizers. Credit participation is measured on the signal listed in Table 4 . (b) Circuit participation against the number of neurons that share one normalization factor, on modular addition at three moduli and on S 5 S_{5} . Error bars show one standard deviation across three seeds.

Circuit concentration is a consequence of the training dynamics and not of the task alone. The concentrated circuits found under backpropagation with Adam are one of several ways a grokked solution can be implemented. A neuron stops contributing when its credit is small relative to the non-gradient term of its update, whether that term is the coupled decay, Adam’s ϵ \epsilon or the decay of a gain, and learning rules that rebalance each neuron keep it in use. The condition also governs MLP units in a 30 30 M-parameter language model trained with Adam and L2 regularization, where balancing each unit’s decay leaves 1.3 % 1.3\% instead of 24 % 24\% nearly unused at lower validation loss, and AdamW leaves 0.9 % 0.9\% , as the condition predicts (Appendix F.8 ). For mechanistic interpretability this means that the size of a circuit found in a trained network, including the circuit that pruning extracts, reflects the learning rule and how weight decay enters it, as well as the task. A sparse circuit read out of a network trained with Adam is a property of that training run, and comparing learning rules separates what the task requires from what the optimizer selected. A distributed circuit loses less when units are removed, as under a hardware fault, while pruning and fine-tuning profit from the nearly unused neurons of a concentrated circuit, which can be removed at no cost or recruited by a related task that needs new hidden features. On modular addition, the choice of learning rule trades robustness to neuron loss against compressibility and spare capacity, without changing the learned algorithm.

The theory isolates the distribution mechanism in a simplified linear model without adaptive normalization and covers rescalings that preserve update directions. The results on nonlinear networks and on optimizers are empirical. Under AdamW without decay on normalization parameters the remaining effect is small (participation 0.91 0.91 to 0.96 0.96 ) and not explained by the condition, and for Adam’s ϵ \epsilon holding the per-neuron ratio fixed removes about half of the effect. The algorithm checks cover modular addition only. The adaptation advantage appears for targets that need new hidden combinations of the operand frequencies and not for targets that change only the readout. The robustness advantage concerns the deletion of neurons.

passages.text: Modern foundation models are trained through multiple stages, yet how these stages interact and how compute should be allocated across them remain poorly understood. We introduce an analytically tractable high-dimensional model combining unsupervised pretraining with a linear autoencoder, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with noisy stepwise labels, and reinforcement learning (RL) with sparse episodic rewards. Using random matrix theory and an operator-projection closure, we derive approximate low-dimensional learning dynamics that closely match simulations. We show that finite pretraining data imposes a representation-dependent performance limit, with Bayes classification error scaling as the inverse square root of the pretraining sample ratio, and observe the same exponent in asymptotic SFT and RL errors. Better pretraining also reduces sensitivity to noisy supervision. SFT initialization shortens the initial RL plateau induced by sparse rewards, an effect we also observe in OLMo-2 1B on GSM8K. Longer SFT warm starts additionally improve asymptotic RL performance. Optimizing compute across all three stages reveals that the optimal allocation depends on supervision quality and total budget, with a non-monotonic dependence of the RL compute share on budget. Finally, a complementary compositional model shows how RL selectively strengthens task-relevant pretrained skills while largely preserving unused skills. Together, these results identify mechanisms linking representation quality, feedback structure, and compute allocation in multistage training.

—To this end, we develop an analytically tractable high-dimensional model based on statistical physics Seung et al. (1992) ; Saad and Solla (1995) ; Zdeborová and Krzakala (2016) . The model isolates the effects of pretrained representation quality, dense stepwise supervision, and sparse episodic rewards. We derive deterministic learning dynamics in the high-dimensional limit and obtain a tractable, approximately closed system of ODEs, allowing us to study how pretrained representations, supervision quality, and compute allocation jointly determine downstream performance. Our contributions are: • We combine random matrix theory with an operator-projection closure to obtain a low-dimensional approximation of the SFT and RL dynamics, validated against simulations. We derive the α − 1 / 2 \alpha^{-1/2} scaling of the representation-dependent Bayes error with pretraining sample size and observe the same exponent in asymptotic finetuning error. • We characterize how SFT and RL complement each other. SFT shortens the initial sparse-reward plateau, an effect also observed in OLMo-2 1B on GSM8K. Under spherical normalization and locally optimal learning rates, longer SFT warm starts additionally improve asymptotic RL performance. Better pretraining also reduces the excess SFT error caused by label noise. • We optimize compute allocation across pretraining, SFT, and RL. The optimal split depends on both supervision quality and the total budget: noisier labels favour RL, while the optimal RL share can vary non-monotonically with total compute. • We extend the model to compositional tasks, showing how prior skill proficiency accelerates RL and how finetuning selectively improves task-relevant skills while largely preserving unused skills.

The problem of anisotropic data covariance generating an infinite hierarchy of order parameters has been studied in the context of online learning with structured data Yoshida and Okada (2019) . In that work, the authors show that the ODE system can only be closed if the covariance has a finite number of unique eigenvalues, where there is a pair of order parameters associated to every unique eigenvalue. There are several works that address this feature: approaches include replacing the infinite discrete hierarchy by a closed functional object — a spectral order parameter ( Goldt et al., 2020 ; Goldt et al., 2022 ) or a resolvent ( Collins-Woodfin et al., 2024 ) . However, this is non-trivial to implement in the case of a random data covariance. Another more recent approach most similar in spirit to ours is Xu et al. (2026) , where the authors show the infinite hierarchy can be exponentially well approximated by a finite truncated system. Ours is merely a different method of truncation, without a proof of exponential convergence.

Figure 1 : (a) A Schematic of multistage training pipeline. Each solid trapezoid indicates a single linear neural network layer. Pretraining is a Linear Autoencoder (LAE) that approximately learns the principal subspace of data 𝐱 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , Σ ) \mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) , where Σ \Sigma is equal to the identity apart from a noise subspace, with identity covariance scaled by Δ < 1 \Delta<1 . C PT C_{\text{PT}} is the compute allocated to pretraining. In the subsequent finetuning (SFT and RL), a teacher network 𝐰 ∗ \mathbf{w}^{*} gives labels y ∗ y^{*} from the signal subspace and it is used to train a student network 𝐰 \mathbf{w} learning in the subspace of the LAE encoder projection with feedback. The student predicts label y y using the effective features 𝐱 ~ \tilde{\mathbf{x}} . Importantly, SFT is modelled by every observation at each t t updating the student, while RL is modelled by bulk feedback through reward at the end of a ‘correct’ sequence through the entire t = 1 , … , T t=1,\dots,T episode. We denote the compute allocations to SFT and RL, C SFT C_{\text{SFT}} and C RL C_{\text{RL}} respectively. (b) Optimal generalisation performance against total Compute flops under three protocols: SFT only, RL only, and SFT with RL. Compute is allocated as described in 5.1 , parameters are set as in 5 d.

Limitations : Our model is a simplified and abstract setup, where each component is modeled as a simple single-layer network. The real-world models rely on complex architectures and heavy engineering, which we do not account for. Our proposed model of RL captures an aspect of bulk feedback in RL, but it assumes independence between all observations in an episode. In practice, the cost of SFT is not just a compute one, but the cost of being able to source enough high quality supervision data we do not take into account the difficulty of obtaining the labels of the data for defining compute budget in our analysis. Using frozen encoder weights is a simplification, in practice all weights are updated during fine-tuning.

Only experiments that required a considerable compute resources was LLM experiment with OlMO 1B model and GSM8k dataset in Figure 3 b. All of the LLM experiments were run on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. A RL run with our setup took 8 hours, whereas SFT completed in under 1 hour.

passages.section: Do Pretraining Optimizer Gains Transfer to KL Distillation?
passages.text: Lavinia Ghita * Dhruv Desai * Affiliation: NVIDIA * * footnotetext: Equal contribution. Emails: lghita@nvidia.com , dhruvd@nvidia.com . Abstract. Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student–teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality–trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.

Prior work on Shampoo, SOAP, Muon, and related matrix-structured optimizers reports data-efficiency or wall-clock gains over AdamW in language-model pretraining [ 1 , 6 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Those comparisons concern long-horizon next-token training from random initialization, with outcomes sensitive to model scale, batch size, parameterization, and hyperparameter transfer [ 3 , 10 , 11 ] . KL distillation instead starts from an instruction-tuned student and uses the teacher’s full next-token probability distribution, rather than a one-hot target, at every supervised token. It also runs for a comparatively short horizon, while online teacher inference reduces the optimizer’s share of trainer time. Consequently, an optimizer advantage in pretraining does not necessarily imply lower validation KL per training step or per unit of trainer time in short-horizon distillation. Within each student–teacher pair, all recipes share the tokenizer, data, forward-KL objective, batch size, and training budget; we compare minimum validation KL within budget, validation KL at matched steps, and trainer time. Canonical two-sided Shampoo [ 1 ] cannot be applied uniformly to the evaluated matrix geometries under the factor-dimension cap. We therefore derive a scalar-row-mean quarter-power reduction and compare it with a right-only half-power reduction based on Scalable Shampoo’s one-sided construction [ 3 ] , treating both as specific feasible recipes rather than family-wide representatives.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 defines the distillation objective and optimizer recipes, including the Shampoo reductions. Section 3 describes the experimental design, and Section 4 reports fixed-budget quality, optimization trajectories, and trainer time. Section 5 discusses interpretation and limitations, and Section 6 concludes. Appendix A documents implementation fidelity, Appendix B grafting, and Appendix C hyperparameter selection.

Trainer-time results sharpen the quality comparison: every matrix-structured method with completed results adds trainer time relative to AdamW, whereas AdaGrad becomes slightly faster than AdamW at the larger evaluated student sizes (Figure 3 ). This is consistent with AdaGrad’s lighter elementwise update: it maintains one accumulator rather than AdamW’s first- and second-moment states, reducing optimizer-state traffic and pointwise work. Online teacher inference, validation, and checkpointing reduce the optimizer’s share of total time. These ratios therefore measure systems-level protocol overhead, not student-only optimizer-kernel overhead, and may understate the latter.

At Qwen2.5 32 ​ B ← 72 ​ B 32\mathrm{B}\leftarrow 72\mathrm{B} , SOAP incurred substantially greater trainer time than AdamW without a clear improvement in validation KL at the matched 561-step horizon. Model sharding does not distribute this optimizer work, so we did not extend SOAP.

The transfer gap may reflect the shift from long-horizon pretraining to short-horizon distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. Matrix-structured methods add estimation and refresh costs, leaving less opportunity for quality gains to offset trainer-time overhead; the study does not isolate these mechanisms causally. That reversal comes from approximations that retain different information and exponents, with factor coverage and selected hyperparameters that also vary across pairs. The SOAP and Muon conclusions are similarly tied to routing and implementation choices. All-2D Muon differs from the hidden-layer-only reference recipe, and unblocked SOAP differs algorithmically and operationally from blocked distributed alternatives. Moreover, Shampoo and SOAP use observed-gradient moments, which need not approximate the model’s Fisher information matrix [ 17 ] . The findings therefore do not rank optimizer families independently of factorization, routing, and implementation. Limitations. The empirical scope is four dense Qwen student–teacher pairs from two model generations and one chain-of-thought corpus. The study does not test longer schedules, other distillation objectives or data, or sparse model architectures. Validation KL measures teacher matching rather than downstream performance. The evaluated Shampoo recipes are unblocked and use at most one full right matrix factor. Trainer times are specific to the 72- and 144-accelerator GB200 allocations and depend on the evaluated adapters. Qwen2.5 SOAP is deliberately limited to one matched 561-step run and is excluded from full-budget summaries. The study also includes no matched controls initialized from checkpoints pretrained with each evaluated optimizer.

candidates.title: Beyond the Log-Linear Frontier: Pre-Asymptotic Analysis of Finite-Budget Neural Scaling Laws

candidates.title: Train High, Ship Low: Efficient LoRA Synchronization for Distributed On-Policy Post-Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Transmitting LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training over bandwidth-constrained networks. Lowering the training rank may limit the capacity a workload needs, while adaptive optimizer updates are difficult to compress. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. candidates.title: Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks with Sparse Connectivity
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Empirical evidence suggests that large neural networks rarely make effective use of all available parameters, with learned solutions exhibiting pronounced sparsity. candidates.title: Grokking Can Be Steered: Selecting Desirable Solutions By Choice Of Learning Rule
candidates.abstract_excerpt: During grokking, a network transitions from memorization to generalization, yet what shapes the neural implementation (circuit) of the generalizing solution and specifically the number of participating neurons (its size) remains unclear. We find that the learning rule, the combination of credit assignment algorithm and optimizer, controls this: On modular addition, every learning rule we study that groks recovers the same Fourier-based algorithm, yet implemented by circuits that differ in size. Why? A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update, and this single condition unifies three routes to unused neurons: the coupled weight decay, Adam's $ε$ and the decay of a trainable per-neuron gain. Equalizing the magnitude of credit assigned to each neuron, or scaling each neuron's weight decay by its credit, expands the effective circuit size, measured from the outgoing weights, from 60% to 99% of the layer's neurons at similar training and test accuracy. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Denoising generative models predict clean data ($x$), noise ($ε$), or velocity ($v$), while training losses can be measured in any of these spaces. Although the resulting nine combinations are algebraically related, they can yield substantially different denoising accuracy and sample quality. We disentangle the effects of prediction and loss spaces. For a fixed prediction target, we show that changing the loss space is exactly equivalent to timestep reweighting and provide a heuristic analysis of how this reweighting affects generation quality. Combining this bound with prediction-dependent error conversion yields distinct necessary conditions on bottleneck capacity. Experiments with U-Net and JiT across CIFAR-10, Imagenette, and ImageNet-256 support these theoretical predictions. 2611.17191:d224d36762e75b5f46a1f2e4995d7.question: In the mixed-domain LoRA rank sweeps, what are the unpenalized LoRA baselines, model sizes, evaluation metrics, and per-rank results for the Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer? Does higher effective rank consistently improve held-out perplexity without worsening forgetting?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

(B–D) Learning–forgetting trade-offs: Train PPL (mixture learning) versus Wiki PPL, StarCoder PPL (pretraining proxies), and WMT CS–EN PPL (in-mixture translation retention); lower-left is better. The three Rényi-2 penalty points use different regularization weights λ \lambda . Standard LoRA training often underutilizes its allocated subspace so nominal rank is an unreliable proxy for usable adapter capacity in the learning–forgetting trade-off. We proposed effective-rank maximization via the Rényi-2 penalty, a parameterization-agnostic, SVD-free term added to the language-modeling loss, and showed across mixed-domain SFT, task-specific SFT, rank sweeps, and scheduling ablations that it can reduce forgetting on pretraining proxies while maintaining competitive target-task fit. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models, λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA, with mean Train PPL improving or increasing by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one comparison. Our single-task and scheduling experiments also demonstrate configuration-dependent learning and retention outcomes: the penalty can improve retention without a large training-fit cost, but does not eliminate the learning–forgetting trade-off. Spectral diagnostics provide descriptive comparisons of the resulting updates. Effective rank is therefore not merely a post-hoc diagnostic but a trainable objective that regularizes toward fuller utilization.

Wiki PPL and StarCoder PPL are reference-probe perplexities on fixed OLMo-Mix-1124 slices, using the plain-text supervision protocol and batch limits specified above. In the mixed-domain setting we additionally log in-mixture retention probes on held-out GSM8K and WMT19 Czech–English validation text; Appendix Table 5 reports both in-mixture probes. eRank is the Roy–Vetterli effective rank of the accumulated adapter update Δ ​ W \Delta W , averaged over all targeted down_proj modules, taken from the last logged rank diagnostic. This is distinct from the Rényi-2 surrogate used in the objective. Dense down-projection fine-tuning baselines select hyperparameters via a separate sweep (Section F.1 ), but reported metrics still refer to the terminal state of the selected run. Post-hoc spectral analyses (intruder dimensions, subspace alignment, singular-direction mixing) use measurements from the final saved checkpoint.

2611.16905:d36e62e78cd73fe93a49f96f205e8.question: In LLM pretraining experiments, what model sizes, token budgets, hardware, and baselines are used to compare FOAM with SOAP, Muon, and AdamW? What are the measured optimizer-state memory, peak GPU memory, wall-clock throughput, and validation-loss results, and are comparisons made at matched training compute?

passages.text: Second-order optimizers ( e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP’s dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP’s dense second moment, and we measure only a 15–20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP’s optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP’s gains need not require SOAP’s cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam . $\star$ $\star$ footnotetext: Correspondence to {jaemyung.yu, dongyoon.han}@navercorp.com

Concretely, our approach is built on two structural simplifications: input-only preconditioning and a factored Adam-Moment update. The first simplification drops the output-side factor L L and retains only the input-side factor R R , eliminating its m 2 m^{2} memory and one of the two eigendecompositions. Its justification follows from the Kronecker structure of the Hessian, in which all output rows of an affine layer share the same input-side outer product x ​ x ⊤ xx^{\top} [ 25 ] , while the Hessian of transformer layers is empirically near-block-diagonal along output neurons or heads [ 50 ] , making the input-only form the natural one-sided approximation. The second simplification replaces the dense rotated second moment with a row-and-column factored estimator, r ∈ ℝ m r\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and c ∈ ℝ n c\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , with trace normalization, reducing the buffer size from m ​ n mn to m + n m+n . Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption [ 35 ] with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP’s dense second moment, and the K-FAC part holds to a 15 15 – 20 % 20\% relative error in practice. Together, these simplifications reduce SOAP’s optimizer state from 2 ​ m ​ n + 2 ​ m 2 + 2 ​ n 2 2mn+2m^{2}+2n^{2} to m ​ n + 2 ​ n 2 + m + n mn+2n^{2}+m+n and the amortized eigendecomposition count from two to one. We call the resulting method FOAM ( F actored O ne-sided A dam- M oment).

Figure 1 highlights FOAM’s main advantages. On pre-training, FOAM matches the strong Muon and SOAP baselines on validation loss with half of SOAP’s optimizer state and reaches AdamW’s final loss within 7 % 7\% of AdamW’s own wall-clock time , while SOAP needs more than twice as long at 760M, and FOAM matches AdamW’s hyperparameter robustness over a three-fold learning-rate range. The advantage holds from 124M to 760M parameters with learning rates re-tuned at every size from a μ \mu P [ 46 ] anchor. In summary, our contributions are: (i) a structural justification of input-only preconditioning, with the Kronecker structure of the Hessian and empirical verifications with LLMs with recent architectural elements; (ii) a factored Adam-Moment update with trace normalization, exact under K-FAC with a diagonal output curvature and empirically validated through K-FAC-residual measurements during training; and (iii) the resulting algorithm FOAM, a scalable and practical SOAP variant that delivers SOAP-class quality with half of SOAP’s optimizer state ( + 7.4 % +7.4\% measured peak training memory over AdamW) and Muon-class wall-clock time.

Table 2 reports the main pre-training results across three model scales. SOAP attains the lowest validation loss at every scale, with FOAM behind by 0.004 0.004 , 0.008 0.008 , and 0.005 0.005 nats at small, medium, and large, each within about one seed std. FOAM is ahead of Muon, AdaMuon, and AdamW at every scale. The cost gap to SOAP widens at scale . FOAM uses half of SOAP’s matrix-parameter state at every size, and its measured peak memory at small size is + 7.4 % +7.4\% over AdamW against + 12.9 % +12.9\% for SOAP. On wall-clock time, FOAM needs fewer steps than AdamW to reach AdamW’s final loss, which offsets its higher per-step cost: its time to that loss, t A t_{\mathrm{A}} , is within 7 % 7\% of AdamW’s own at every scale and equal at large ( 10.53 10.53 vs. 10.55 10.55 h), whereas SOAP needs 1.35 × 1.35\times at small and 2.15 × 2.15\times at large, as its two eigendecompositions grow cubically with width.

Limitations and future work. Our experiments stop at GPT-2 scale, up to 1.56B parameters, so whether FOAM’s advantages hold for frontier-scale pre-training remains the main open question. Our implementation does not yet shard R R and Q R Q_{R} across devices, which matters at the ≥ 7 \geq 7 B scale, although the layer-wise distributed optimizer of Khona et al. [22] suggests that this is an engineering rather than a fundamental obstacle. The factored update is least accurate at the key projection, whose gradients pass through RoPE and softmax (Appendix C ). Finally, the embeddings and the lm-head stay on AdamW because their vocabulary dimension rules out a dense factor on that side, although a FOAM-style factor on their small hidden dimension would be affordable. Extending FOAM to these layers, and attention-aware factorizations for the key projection, are natural next steps. When to use FOAM. FOAM fits when SOAP-class quality is needed but SOAP’s memory or wall-clock is binding, since it stays within 0.004 0.004 – 0.008 0.008 nats of SOAP at half its optimizer state and, at 760M, about half its wall-clock. Against Muon and AdaMuon, quality slightly favors FOAM at every scale and speed is near parity, while AdaMuon keeps less state. Muon and AdaMuon thus remain preferable when optimizer state is the hardest constraint. Second-order optimizers ( e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP’s dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP’s dense second moment, and we measure only a 15–20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP’s optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP’s gains need not require SOAP’s cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam . $\star$ $\star$ footnotetext: Correspondence to {jaemyung.yu, dongyoon.han}@navercorp.com

Concretely, our approach is built on two structural simplifications: input-only preconditioning and a factored Adam-Moment update. The first simplification drops the output-side factor L L and retains only the input-side factor R R , eliminating its m 2 m^{2} memory and one of the two eigendecompositions. Its justification follows from the Kronecker structure of the Hessian, in which all output rows of an affine layer share the same input-side outer product x ​ x ⊤ xx^{\top} [ 25 ] , while the Hessian of transformer layers is empirically near-block-diagonal along output neurons or heads [ 50 ] , making the input-only form the natural one-sided approximation. The second simplification replaces the dense rotated second moment with a row-and-column factored estimator, r ∈ ℝ m r\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and c ∈ ℝ n c\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , with trace normalization, reducing the buffer size from m ​ n mn to m + n m+n . Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption [ 35 ] with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP’s dense second moment, and the K-FAC part holds to a 15 15 – 20 % 20\% relative error in practice. Together, these simplifications reduce SOAP’s optimizer state from 2 ​ m ​ n + 2 ​ m 2 + 2 ​ n 2 2mn+2m^{2}+2n^{2} to m ​ n + 2 ​ n 2 + m + n mn+2n^{2}+m+n and the amortized eigendecomposition count from two to one.
